notes.fundi: Anyone skilled with their hands: fundi wa magari (mechanic), fundi cherehani (tailor).
notes.omusuubuzi: Literally “one who does business”. Many: wafanyabiashara.
notes.anafanya: With kazi: anafanya kazi, he or she works.

guidebook.intro: Ask anyone in East Africa what they do and you may hear about two or three jobs at once. Learn to name jobs and say who does what.

tips.title: Job words: m- and wa-
body: Many words for people start with **m-** (one) and **wa-** (many), and several are built from a verb: **-lima** (farm) gives **mkulima**, **-pika** (cook) gives **mpishi**.
Borrowed words like **dereva** and **askari** don’t change, but they still agree like people: **dereva wangu**, **askari wawili**.

tips.title: Who is doing it
body: The front of a verb says who: **ni-** (I), **u-** (you), **a-** (he or she), **tu-** (we), **m-** (you all), **wa-** (they). Then comes the tense, **-na-** for now, then the verb.
So **ninafanya** is “I do”, **anafanya** “she does” and **wanafanya** “they do”. Swahili has no separate word for “he” and “she”: **a-** is both.

culture.title: Jua kali
body: In Kenya, **jua kali** (“hot sun”) is the name for the informal workers who build, weld and fix things in open-air workshops. A **fundi** there can mend almost anything.
